attribution.note: Marcus's own footnote in his post, not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: The revised wording keeps 'virtually all', 'really on the scene', 'very few really envision' and his 'and so' link. It is a firm observation about the existing body of law.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary: most law predates modern AI, and few laws deliberately address it. The global scope and lack of a cutoff are flagged. Requiring an inventory of the full legal corpus is demanding but fair to his words.

evidence.note: Stanford HAI, before the post: 123 AI-related bills since 2016. There is no count of all laws to compare against, so it cannot show what share of laws is AI-related.
Official CAC generative-AI measures, in force 15 Aug 2023. One AI-specific instrument; it says nothing about the share of all laws.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows that AI-specific laws existed, but it gives no count of all laws in force, no spread of drafting dates, and no measure of which laws substantively anticipate AI. The support and contradiction conditions both need such an inventory. Neither item settles the proportions, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in the post's opening paragraph.

semantics.note: 'On the ropes' means the Act was seriously threatened. 'In danger of failing' captures that without implying certain failure.

contract.note: The ordinary reading (a serious threat, not certain failure) matches the idiom. The window up to publication is reasonable, and the support condition asks for a serious impasse rather than routine friction.

evidence.note: IAPP, 15 Nov 2023, interviewing negotiators: reports a recent 'fallout', foundation models as the 'most difficult' issue, and 6 Dec as the real test of the Act's fate. This points to a serious threat to agreement.
Mozilla, 20 Nov 2023, describes gridlock that could derail the Act but sees room for compromise. This fits 'on the ropes' and argues against reading it as certain failure.

reviews.rationale: Reports from mid to late November 2023, quoting participants, describe a breakdown over foundation models serious enough to put the Act's fate at stake in the 6 Dec trilogue. That meets the support condition. The view that compromise remained possible fits the claim rather than contradicting it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own parenthetical assertion in the post.

semantics.note: The normalisation accurately extracts the parenthetical figure for cumulative revenue to date and its share of the economy. Leaving out the part about Big Tech's intent is appropriate.

contract.note: Reading 'a few billion' as several billion USD of cumulative realized revenue is ordinary. Under the money-claim rules, the unknown accounting basis rules out a firm verdict; that limit is flagged openly.

evidence.note: Menlo Ventures (an investor's survey), 13 Nov 2023: 2023 enterprise gen-AI spend of about $2.5B. One year of enterprise spending only, not cumulative revenue across the whole sector.
Reuters, 29 Aug 2023: OpenAI's revenue forecast and monthly run rate. Figures for one company, and a forecast or run rate rather than cumulative sector revenue.

reviews.rationale: No item gives cumulative realized generative-AI revenue across providers through 28 Nov 2023, and none supplies an economic denominator. The figures given are one year of enterprise spending and one firm's forecast and run rate. They roughly fit a few billion dollars but cannot settle it, and the accounting basis is unknown. Outcome unresolved.
